title: Open and closed sets
objectives: Prove a set is open or closed, and characterise closed sets by limits of sequences.

screens.title: Room around a point
screens.prose: The set is the open interval $(0, 1)$. Around $x = 0.9$ draw the interval $(0.9 - r, 0.9 + r)$, all points within $r$ of 0.9. Move $r$ and keep that interval inside $(0, 1)$.

derive.caption: $r$ = {{fixed(r, 2)}}: the interval runs from {{fixed(0.9 - r, 2)}} to {{fixed(0.9 + r, 2)}}.

screens.question: Set $r$ to the largest radius that keeps the interval inside $(0, 1)$.

hints.text: Which end of $(0, 1)$ is nearer to 0.9?
The right end, 1, is 0.1 away; the left end is 0.9 away.

feedback.correct: Right. $r = 0.1$: the interval $(0.8, 1)$ just fits, since 1 itself is left out.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the distance from 0.9 to the nearer end of $(0, 1)$.

byKey.wide: Your interval pokes past 1, so it holds points outside the set.
byKey.small: Your interval fits, but a larger one fits too. The largest is $1 - 0.9 = 0.1$.

explain.text: The nearer end is 1, at distance 0.1, so $r = \min(x, 1 - x) = 0.1$. With $r = 0.1$ the interval is $(0.8, 1)$, inside $(0, 1)$ because both are open. Every point of $(0, 1)$ has such room.

screens.title: No room at the edge
screens.prose: Now take the set $[0, 1)$, which includes 0. A point has room in a set if some interval $(x - r, x + r)$ with $r > 0$ fits inside the set.
screens.question: Which radius $r$ gives the point 0 room in $[0, 1)$?

options.text: None: every $(-r, r)$ holds negative numbers, which are outside $[0, 1)$.
Any $r < 1$, since $[0, 1)$ has length 1.
options.why: You measured the length of the set. Room is about both sides of 0, and the left side is empty.

options.text: A tiny one, such as $r = 0.0001$.
options.why: $(-0.0001, 0.0001)$ still holds $-0.00005$, which is negative.
With $r = 0$ the interval $(0, 0)$ is empty and holds nothing. Room needs $r > 0$.

hints.text: Look to the left of 0.
Every interval $(-r, r)$ with $r > 0$ holds $-\tfrac r2$.
And $-\tfrac r2 \notin [0, 1)$.

feedback.correct: Right. 0 has no room, so $[0, 1)$ is not open.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the left half of $(-r, r)$ for every $r > 0$.

explain.text: Every $(-r, r)$ with $r > 0$ contains $-\tfrac r2 \notin [0, 1)$. So the point 0 has no room. A set is **open** when every one of its points has room; $[0, 1)$ is not.

screens.title: Room in a disc
screens.prose: In the plane with the straight-line metric, the **open ball** $B(x, r) = \{y : d(x, y) < r\}$ is a disc. Take the open unit disc $B(0, 1)$ and the point $p = (0.6, 0.7)$ inside it.

state.caption: The dashed ray runs from 0 through $p$ to the edge.

screens.question: What is the largest $r$ with $B(p, r)$ inside the disc? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: How far is $p$ from the centre 0?
The room left is $1 - \sqrt{0.85}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract $p$'s distance from the centre from the radius 1.

byKey.dist: You gave $p$'s distance from 0. The room is what is left of the radius, $1 - 0.9220$.
byKey.coord: You used the nearer edge of the square $|x_i| < 1$. The disc's edge is closer, along the ray from 0.

explain.text: If $d(p, y) < 1 - \sqrt{0.85}$, then $d(0, y) \le d(0, p) + d(p, y) < 1$, by the triangle inequality. So $B(p, 0.0780)$ fits, and no larger ball does, along the ray. Every point of the open disc has such room, so the disc is open.

screens.title: Room in a square
screens.prose: Now use the largest-gap metric $d_\infty$. Its open unit ball $B(0, 1) = \{y : \max(|y_1|, |y_2|) < 1\}$ is an open square, and its balls are squares too. Take the same $p = (0.6, 0.7)$.

state.caption: A square ball of radius 0.3 around $p$.

screens.question: What is the largest $r$ with $B_\infty(p, r)$ inside the square?

hints.text: A square ball of radius $r$ reaches $r$ in each coordinate.
The gaps to the edges are $1 - 0.6 = 0.4$ and $1 - 0.7 = 0.3$.
The nearer edge wins: $\min(0.4, 0.3)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the gap from $p$ to the nearest edge of the square.

byKey.other: You used the right edge, 0.4 away. The top edge is nearer, at 0.3.
byKey.disc: That was the disc. In the square the corners are farther away, so there is more room.

explain.text: The ball $B_\infty(p, r)$ is the square $(0.6 \pm r) \times (0.7 \pm r)$. It fits while $0.7 + r \le 1$ and $0.6 + r \le 1$, so $r = 0.3$. Here the square drawn touches the top edge, which the open square leaves out.

screens.title: Open and closed sets
screens.prose: In a metric space $(X, d)$, a set $U$ is **open** if every $x \in U$ has some $r > 0$ with $B(x, r) \subseteq U$. A set $F$ is **closed** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is open.
screens.question: Why is every open ball $B(x, r)$ an open set?

options.text: For $y$ in the ball, $B(y, r - d(x, y)) \subseteq B(x, r)$, by the triangle inequality.
Because it is called an open ball.
options.why: A name proves nothing. Each point $y$ of the ball needs its own smaller ball inside.

options.text: For $y$ in the ball, $B(y, r) \subseteq B(x, r)$.
options.why: A ball of the full radius $r$ round $y$ pokes out when $y$ is near the edge. Shrink it to $r - d(x, y)$.

options.text: Because $d(x, y) < r$ is strict.
options.why: Strictness is needed, but it is not the argument. We still need a ball round $y$ that fits.

hints.text: Take $y$ with $d(x, y) < r$. How much room is left?
Try $s = r - d(x, y) > 0$.
If $d(y, z) < s$, then $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z) < r$.

feedback.correct: Right. Room $r - d(x, y)$, by the triangle inequality.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a radius for a ball round $y$ that stays inside $B(x, r)$.

explain.text: Let $s = r - d(x, y) > 0$. If $d(y, z) < s$, then $d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z) < d(x, y) + s = r$. So $B(y, s) \subseteq B(x, r)$, which is the disc picture with $s = 0.0780$.

screens.title: A limit outside a closed set
screens.prose: Let $F$ be closed, $x_n \in F$ for all $n$, and $x_n \to x$. Suppose $x \notin F$. Then $x$ lies in the open set $X \setminus F$, so some ball $B(x, r)$ misses $F$ entirely.
screens.question: Why is that a contradiction?

options.text: $x_n \to x$ puts $x_n$ in $B(x, r)$ for all $n \ge N$, yet every $x_n$ is in $F$, which the ball misses.
Limits of points in $F$ are always in $F$.
options.why: That is what we are proving. Assuming it is circular.

options.text: $B(x, r)$ is open, so it cannot miss a closed set.
options.why: Open sets can miss closed sets: $(2, 3)$ misses $[0, 1]$. The contradiction comes from the terms $x_n$.

options.text: The limit is unique, so $x \in F$.
options.why: Uniqueness of limits says nothing about where the limit lies.

hints.text: Use the definition of $x_n \to x$ with $\varepsilon = r$.
For $n \ge N$, $d(x_n, x) < r$, so $x_n \in B(x, r)$.
But $x_n \in F$ and $B(x, r) \cap F = \varnothing$.

feedback.correct: Right. A ball round the limit holds all late terms, so it cannot miss $F$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the definition of convergence with $\varepsilon = r$.

explain.text: Convergence with $\varepsilon = r$ puts every $x_n$ with $n \ge N$ inside $B(x, r)$. Those $x_n$ are in $F$, but the ball misses $F$. So $x \in F$ after all.

screens.title: Closed sets keep their limits
screens.prose: Prove: if $F$ is closed, then $F$ contains the limit of every convergent sequence of its points. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $x_n \in F$ with $x_n \to x$, and suppose $x \notin F$.
$X \setminus F$ is open and contains $x$, so some $B(x, r)$ lies in $X \setminus F$.
Since $x_n \to x$, there is $N$ with $d(x_n, x) < r$, so $x_N \in B(x, r)$.
Then $x_N \notin F$, contradicting $x_N \in F$. So $x \in F$. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: Every limit has that property, closed set or not: each ball round 0 meets $(0, 1]$. So it cannot be the reason.

hints.text: Argue by contradiction: suppose the limit escapes.
Closed means the complement is open, so a ball round $x$ misses $F$.
Convergence puts a term in that ball.

feedback.correct: Right. Suppose, open complement, a term in the ball, contradiction.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Suppose $x \notin F$, use the open complement, then convergence.

byKey.d1: You concluded from balls meeting $F$. That is the other direction's idea, and it needs closedness to finish.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: The proof uses closed only through its definition, an open complement. On $(0, 1]$, which is not closed, $\tfrac1n \to 0 \notin (0, 1]$. So the hypothesis is needed.

screens.title: Keeping limits makes a set closed
screens.prose: Prove the converse: if $F$ contains the limit of every convergent sequence of its points, then $F$ is closed. We show $X \setminus F$ is open. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $X \setminus F$ is not open: some $x \notin F$ has every ball $B(x, r)$ meeting $F$.
For each $n$, pick $x_n \in F$ with $d(x_n, x) < \tfrac1n$.
By hypothesis the limit $x$ lies in $F$, contradicting $x \notin F$. So $X \setminus F$ is open and $F$ is closed. $\blacksquare$
Pick one point $y \in F$ near $x$; then $x = y$.
lines.why: One nearby point says nothing about $x$. We need points ever closer, a sequence tending to $x$.

hints.text: Negate 'the complement is open' at one point $x$.
Every ball round $x$ meets $F$; use radii $\tfrac1n$.
Those points form a sequence in $F$ tending to $x$.

feedback.correct: Right. Negate openness, pick a point in each $B(x, \tfrac1n)$, and the limit lands in $F$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Negate, pick $x_n$ in shrinking balls, show $x_n \to x$, contradict.

byKey.d1: You picked one point. The proof needs a whole sequence, one point in each ball $B(x, \tfrac1n)$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: Not open at $x$ means every ball round $x$ meets $F$. Radii $\tfrac1n$ give a sequence in $F$ tending to $x$, by Archimedes. So closed sets are exactly the sets that keep their limits.

screens.title: Adding the missing limit
screens.prose: Let $A = \{1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots\}$ and $B = A \cup \{0\}$, as subsets of $\mathbb{R}$.
screens.question: Which is closed?

options.text: $B$ is closed and $A$ is not, since $\tfrac1n \to 0 \notin A$.
Both: each is a list of separate points.
options.why: Separate points can crowd towards a limit. $A$ misses its limit 0.

options.text: $A$ is closed and $B$ is not, since adding 0 adds a limit point.
options.why: You flipped it. Adding the missing limit is what makes the set closed.

options.text: Neither, since neither is an interval.
options.why: Closed sets need not be intervals. $B$ contains the limit of each of its convergent sequences.

hints.text: Find a sequence in $A$ that converges.
$\tfrac1n \to 0$, and 0 is not in $A$.
In $B$, every convergent sequence tends to 0 or is eventually constant.

feedback.correct: Right. $A$ misses the limit 0; $B$ keeps it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each set with the sequence $\tfrac1n$.

explain.text: $\tfrac1n \in A$ tends to $0 \notin A$, so $A$ is not closed. A convergent sequence in $B$ either tends to 0, which is in $B$, or is eventually constant. So $B$ is closed.

screens.title: Not open is not closed
screens.prose: Open and closed are not opposites. A set can be one, the other, both or neither.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are neither open nor closed?

options.text: $\mathbb{Q}$

options.why: Its complement $(-\infty, 1.5) \cup (2, \infty)$ is open, so it is closed.
Every point has room, so it is open.

options.text: $\mathbb{R}$
options.why: $\mathbb{R}$ is both open and closed, not neither.

hints.text: Test each set twice: does every point have room, and does it keep its limits?
$[0, 1)$ fails at 0 for open, and loses the limit of $1 - \tfrac1n$.
$\mathbb{Q}$ has no room anywhere and loses $\sqrt2$ as a limit of rationals.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each set, test open and closed separately.

byKey.cl: You read 'not open' as closed in reverse. $[1.5, 2]$ is closed: its complement is open.
byKey.op: $(0, 1)$ is open; it is just not closed.

explain.text: $[0, 1)$ is not open at 0 and not closed, since $1 - \tfrac1n \to 1$. $\mathbb{Q}$ holds no interval, and rationals tend to $\sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}$. 'Not open, so closed' is the trap.

screens.title: Unions and intersections
screens.prose: Any union of open sets is open. A point of the union lies in one of them, and its ball there will do. Now intersect the open sets $(-\tfrac1n, \tfrac1n)$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$
screens.question: What is $\bigcap_n (-\tfrac1n, \tfrac1n)$, and is it open?

options.text: $\{0\}$, which is not open.
$\varnothing$, which is open.
options.why: 0 lies in every interval, so the intersection is not empty.

options.text: $\{0\}$, which is open as an intersection of open sets.
options.why: Only finite intersections stay open. No ball $(-r, r)$ fits inside $\{0\}$.

options.text: A tiny open interval round 0.
options.why: Any $x \ne 0$ has $|x| > \tfrac1n$ for large $n$, by Archimedes, so it drops out.

hints.text: Which points lie in every interval?
0 does. For $x \ne 0$, pick $n > \tfrac1{|x|}$.
So only 0 survives. Does $\{0\}$ contain a ball round 0?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find which points lie in every interval, then test openness.

explain.text: For $x \ne 0$, some $n$ has $\tfrac1n < |x|$, so $x$ drops out. The intersection is $\{0\}$, which contains no ball. Two open sets do intersect to an open set: take the smaller of the two radii.

screens.title: Constraints an optimiser can trust
screens.prose: A two-asset book has weights $w = (w_1, w_2)$ with $w_1 + w_2 = 1$. Its volatility $\sigma(w)$ is continuous in $w$ and takes every value from 8% to 20%. The optimiser walks through portfolios $w^{(n)}$ and keeps their limit.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which constraint sets are closed?

options.text: Long-only: $w_1 + w_2 = 1$ and $w_1, w_2 \ge 0$.
$w_1 + w_2 = 1$ and $\sigma(w) \le 0.1$.
Strictly positive: $w_1 + w_2 = 1$ and $w_1, w_2 > 0$.
options.why: The drawn sequence stays in this set and tends to $(0, 1)$, which is not in it.
A strict risk limit can be approached and never met: a limit of portfolios may sit exactly at 10%.

hints.text: Weak inequalities survive limits; strict ones may not.
If $w^{(n)}_1 \ge 0$ for all $n$, then $\lim w^{(n)}_1 \ge 0$.
Continuity of $\sigma$ passes $\sigma(w^{(n)}) \le 0.1$ to the limit.

feedback.correct: Right. The sets written with $\le$ and $=$ are closed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether a limit of portfolios in each set stays in the set.

byKey.pos: You accepted strict positivity. The drawn sequence leaves it in the limit, at $(0, 1)$.
byKey.strict: You accepted a strict limit. Portfolios at 9.9%, 9.99%, ... can tend to one at exactly 10%.

explain.text: Limits keep $=$ and $\le$, and continuity of $\sigma$ carries the risk bound across. So long-only weights and a $\le$ risk limit give closed sets. With $>$ or $<$, an optimiser can creep towards the boundary and find no optimum inside the set.

ideas: Open: every point has a ball $B(x, r)$ inside the set. In $(0, 1)$ the largest radius is $\min(x, 1 - x)$; in $[0, 1)$ the point 0 has none.
Closed: the complement is open. Equivalently, the set keeps the limit of every convergent sequence of its points: $\{\tfrac1n\}$ is not closed, $\{\tfrac1n\} \cup \{0\}$ is.
Unions of open sets are open; finite intersections too, but $\bigcap (-\tfrac1n, \tfrac1n) = \{0\}$ is not. $[0, 1)$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ are neither open nor closed.

formula.name: Closed by sequences
formula.tex: F \text{ closed} \iff \big(x_n \in F,\ x_n \to x \Rightarrow x \in F\big)
formula.note: A ball round an escaped limit would hold every late term, yet miss $F$.

summary.trap: Open and closed are not opposites: $[0, 1)$ is neither, and $\mathbb{R}$ and $\varnothing$ are both.

quiz.prose: Take the open interval $(2, 5)$ and the point $x = 4.5$.
quiz.question: What is the largest $r$ with $(x - r, x + r) \subseteq (2, 5)$?

feedback.correct: Right. $r = 0.5$, set by the nearer end 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the distance from 4.5 to each end and take the smaller.

byKey.far: You used the far end, 2. The near end, 5, is only 0.5 away.
byKey.len: You gave the length of the interval, 3.

explain.text: The ends are 2.5 and 0.5 away. The ball must fit on both sides, so $r = \min(2.5, 0.5) = 0.5$. Every point has some room, so $(2, 5)$ is open.

quiz.prose: Use the discrete metric on $\mathbb{R}$: $d(x, y) = 1$ for $x \ne y$.
quiz.question: Which subsets are open?

options.text: Every subset, since $B(x, \tfrac12) = \{x\}$ fits inside any set holding $x$.
The same ones as usual, such as $(0, 1)$ but not $[0, 1]$.
options.why: Openness depends on the metric. Here $B(0, \tfrac12) = \{0\} \subseteq [0, 1]$.

options.text: Only $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb{R}$.
options.why: $\{0\}$ is open: its one point has the ball $B(0, \tfrac12) = \{0\}$ inside.

options.text: Only the finite subsets.
options.why: Any union of open sets is open, and every set is a union of single points.

feedback.correct: Right. Every set is open, so every set is closed too.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the ball $B(x, \tfrac12)$ in this metric.

explain.text: A ball of radius $\tfrac12$ holds only its centre, since all other distances are 1. So every point of any set has room, and every set is open. Complements are open too, so every set is also closed.

quiz.prose: In any metric space $X$, consider $\varnothing$ and $X$ itself.
quiz.question: Why is $\varnothing$ open?

options.text: It has no points, so 'every point has a ball inside' holds with nothing to check.
Because it is closed.
options.why: Being closed does not stop a set from being open, but it is no reason either. Openness is checked point by point.

options.text: Because $B(x, 0) = \varnothing$.
options.why: Radii must be positive, and $\varnothing$ has no centre $x$ to use.

options.text: It is not open; it is only closed.
options.why: $\varnothing$ is open vacuously, and closed because its complement $X$ is open.

feedback.correct: Right. A statement about every point of an empty set is true.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which points of $\varnothing$ need a ball.

explain.text: 'For every $x \in \varnothing$, something' is true, since there is no $x$. So $\varnothing$ is open. $X$ is open too, so each is the complement of an open set, and both are closed.

quiz.prose: $U$ and $V$ are open, and $x \in U \cap V$, with $B(x, 0.3) \subseteq U$ and $B(x, 0.1) \subseteq V$.
quiz.question: What is the largest radius that certainly gives a ball round $x$ inside $U \cap V$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The ball must fit inside both sets.

byKey.big: $B(x, 0.3)$ fits in $U$, but may poke out of $V$.
byKey.sum: Adding radii makes the ball larger, not safer.

explain.text: $B(x, 0.1) \subseteq B(x, 0.3) \subseteq U$ and $B(x, 0.1) \subseteq V$. So radius 0.1 works for the intersection. With infinitely many sets the minimum can be 0, as for $(-\tfrac1n, \tfrac1n)$.
